title: Who decides that Grand Theft Auto is for adults only?
content:
The latest Grand Theft Auto game brings the franchise's trademark violence and adult storytelling to the latest generation of gaming hardware.
But long before its release, examiners at the Games Rating Authority (GRA), based in Stevenage, Hertfordshire, got to play the game to decide its appropriate age rating.
They analysed its content before assigning a PEGI age rating of 18, which covers 38 European territories.
But who decides a game is for adults only, and how do they make that decision?
Video games experience a similar process to films shown in UK cinemas, where examiners from the British Board of Film Classification watch each film before deciding its rating.
But rating games presents a unique challenge.
Modern games can contain huge worlds that take months to explore. Some allow players to make their own choices, meaning two people can have vastly different experiences.
Developers first complete a GRA questionnaire disclosing any contentious content and provide at least two hours of footage, along with transcripts of the game's dialogue.
Examiners study this material, logging timestamps for instances of blood, gore, horror, drug use or bad language.
Lifelong gamer Sadie West joined the GRA believing it would be the dream job: being paid to play games.
She says: "I definitely look at it more analytically when I'm playing here.
"Since I've started here, I play games a lot less at home, but because I play in such a different way at work to what I'm playing at home, I can still enjoy it."
West uses her skills with a controller to explore choices and scenarios that developers may not have captured on video.
She says: "Things like, is there an NPC (non-playable character) that I can go up to, and can I attack them? Can I hurt this person? Or what happens if my character jumps off a bridge?
"Sometimes I die on purpose to see what a character death would look like."
When playing games in her own time West hates hurting NPCs, but admits at work: "Unfortunately I have to be a bit evil sometimes".
She will typically play a game for several days, checking for blood, suggestive costumes and potentially exploitative in-game purchases.
She says: "Once I'm happy that I've seen everything that would impact the rating, I then go through and I write up a report."
That report is kept on record, while a version without plot spoilers is shared online for parents and players to read.
Examiners follow strict classification criteria overseen by a panel that includes child welfare experts and psychologists.

title: How online mocking of antique gates led to a Harry Potter TV opportunity
content:
What started with online criticism ended with an unexpected call from the team behind the new Harry Potter TV series for an antiques dealer.
When Joel Paxton posted a video of a set of gates on social media, he attracted hundreds of comments from people who disliked them.
But among the almost one million people who watched the clip was a set designer, working on HBO's new Harry Potter series.
Soon afterwards, Paxton was contacted about the gates and found himself getting a behind-the-scenes glimpse of one of television's most anticipated productions.
"We had an interesting set of gates that came through the door, and I'd say they're quite a unique piece," said Paxton, who runs Rustique Living in Sandon, Staffordshire.
"We did a little video on that, and it just blew up for some reason."
Among the online comments were reactions ranging from "yuck" to "disgusting", with some social media users questioning why anyone would want to buy the gates.
The attention turned out to be exactly what the business needed.
"One of the set designers got in touch and wanted that set of gates for the new Harry Potter series," Paxton said.
The TV adaptation, which is due to debut at Christmas, stars Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.
Paxton started Rustique Living while studying for a business degree at Keele University.
What began in his parents' front room during the Covid pandemic has since grown into a shop specialising in unusual antiques and furniture.
"Everybody's after something unique, and finding these unique pieces is always tricky, but when you do, you know you've dropped on something really interesting," he said.
The gates certainly caught people's attention.
The video received nearly 950,000 views on Facebook alone before attracting interest from the Harry Potter team.
Paxton later drove the gates to London himself and was given a glimpse behind the scenes of the secretive production.
"It's an interesting experience because you're not allowed certain access into certain places because you can't get spoilers," he said.
"The film industry is very secretive."
The Harry Potter project is not the first production to buy from Rustique Living.
Paxton said the company had also supplied items to programmes including The Traitors and was increasingly receiving inquiries from television and film productions.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a unique and unexpected entertainment development, providing a clear reason for readers to care. The story showcases a small business's success and unexpected connection to a major entertainment project, offering a fresh and engaging narrative.

title: Westside Cowboy named BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026
content:
Westside Cowboy have been announced as BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026.
Jimmy Bradbury, Reuben Haycocks, Aoife Anson O'Connell and Paddy Murphy formed the band in Manchester in 2023 and have since rocketed from the pub circuit to some of the UK's biggest festivals.
The award is presented to an up-and-coming artist or band who has, with the support of BBC Introducing, made a significant impact and has previously been won by Olivia Dean, Myles Smith and Tom Grennan.
Murphy, from Longridge in Lancashire, said the win put them in "good company", with Bradbury, from Shropshire, adding that it was "very flattering".
BBC Introducing supports new musical talent across the UK , providing a platform to propel new artists on to the local and national stage through 30 Introducing shows, three national radio shows and six shows across BBC Radio 1, Radio 1Xtra, Radio 2, 6Music, Radio 3 and Asian Network.
About 72,000 tracks from emerging UK artists supported by BBC Introducing make it on to the airwaves each year.
Westside Cowboy uploaded their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You) to the Introducing platform in November 2024 and had their first play on radio within hours.
The four-piece played in various other bands before coming together to form Westside Cowboy.
Haycocks, O'Connell, and Murphy had met at Manchester's Royal Northern College of Music in 2021 and later got to know Bradbury after meeting him in the nearby Johnny Roadhouse music shop.
Murphy and Bradbury played in surf-rock trio Katz, while Murphy and Haycocks both worked together in noise-pop trio, DieKaiDie, but it was when Bradbury, who was working in the music shop repairing guitars, asked the others if they wanted to start a new band that Westside Cowboy's journey began.
By the time their second single, Shells, was released in April 2025, they had been been selected to play the BBC Introducing stage at Glastonbury Festival, and the song was put on the BBC 6Music playlist.
Their meteoric rise saw seen them appear on BBC music show Later... with Jools Holland in June and their debut album It Goes On was released on Island Records in August, peaking at number five in the UK charts.
Thanking the Introducing network and listeners for their support, Murphy said it was "really cool to be recognised for the music you make".
"We say this a lot, so apologies if we sound like a broken record, [but] it's funny with this band because... we started it with so little pretence or plan," he said.
"So whenever people give us something cool like [this award], it's all a bit surreal because it still feels like a weekend project that we now just get to do way more regularly.
"We're very lucky it's one of those things.
"It's a great bonus to get to do this."
William Wolstenholme, presenter and producer of BBC Introducing in Lancashire & Cumbria, gave the band their first play and said he remembers messaging them to upload the track.
"Over the past two years, Westside Cowboy have become surely the most exciting band in Manchester, and therefore the country," he said.
"They've fast-tracked from the sweaty pubs of the city's student music scene to many of the most famous venues in the country.
